newsitem.title: UK: Court told Grobbelaar, Segers rigged games.
newsitem.headline: Court told Grobbelaar, Segers rigged games.

text.p: Top goalkeepers Bruce Grobbelaar and Hans Segers accepted large sums of money to fix top English soccer games for the benefit of a Far Eastern gambling syndicate, a court heard on Tuesday.

Former soccer star John Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim, known as Richard Lim, paid both Dutch-born Segers and Grobbelaar, but neither goalkeeper knew the other was involved, prosecutor Richard Calvert Smith told the jury.

Grobbelaar, once one of the game's top players who won five league titles for Liverpool, and the three other defendants denied charges of match-rigging on the first day of their trial at Winchester in southern England.

In the first case of its kind in England since 1964, they face charges of conspiring to give and accept corrupt payments to influence first division and premier league games between February 1991 and November 1994.
Zimbabwean-born Grobbelaar is accused of taking 40,000 pounds ($66,900) to influence the outcome of the Liverpool game against Newcastle in November 1993.
"Mr Grobbelaar has admitted to the crime on tape and video, and was party to such an agreement," Calvert Smith said.

He said Segers -- who played for Wimbledon at the time -- paid large amounts of cash into the London branch of the Swiss affiliate of a New York bank on a number of occasions, each time shortly after his side had lost a match.
Segers told police the money came from crimes he had committed when he was a teenager, but Calvert Smith dismissed the explanation as far-fetched.
Fashanu, his wife and Lim had all regularly received large amounts of money from the Far East which the prosecution would argue had been used to finance the match-rigging, he said.

Calvert Smith gave the members of the jury hefty dossiers containing information on telephone calls made by the defendants as well as their bank accounts. The prosecution case is based on 10,000 documents.
The prosecutor said members of the jury might wonder how one player could alone ensure the result desired by gamblers.
"Well, of course, he can't. He may not have the opportunity to do so," he said, noting that a keeper's defenders or the opposing team could foil his attempts.
"That is exactly what happened in a game between Liverpool and Manchester United in January 1994, about which you will hear a good deal," he said.
But goalkeepers were the obvious players to tap, for people seeking to influence a game corruptly, Calvert Smith said.
"Goalkeepers do make a mistake sometimes, so it may be that the odd deliberate mistake may escape attention," he added.
Grobbelaar was known as a brilliant if eccentric goalkeeper whose antics earned him the nickname "clown prince of soccer".
He left Liverpool in August 1994 for Southampton, another English premier league club, but now plays for Plymouth in the second division.
"There is no evidence that Grobbelaar, while taking part in this corrupt scheme, knew there was another goalkeeper involved in such a scheme," said Calvert Smith.

"A great deal turns on telephone contact in this case," he told the jury, saying logs of the calls over the period in question showed Lim and Fashanu were in constant contact with both Segers and Grobbelaar.
Lim was a former accountancy student, involved in buying and selling cars in Britain. He also had an interest in a London restaurant during the period.
The case broke in November 1994 when the Sun newspaper, armed with accusations from former Grobbelaar business partner Chris Vincent, accused the goalkeeper of being corrupt. ($1=.5979 Pound)
